{{Short description|Theory of Japanese history}}
{{Expand Japanese|騎馬民族征服王朝説|date=November 2023}}

The '''Horserider Theory''' is a theory of the origins of Japan.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Edwards |first=Walter |date=1983 |title=Event and Process in the Founding of Japan: The Horserider Theory in Archeological Perspective |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/132294 |journal=Journal of Japanese Studies |volume=9 |issue=2 |pages=265–295 |doi=10.2307/132294 |jstor=132294 |issn=0095-6848|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kirkland |first=J. Russell |date=1981 |title=The "Horseriders" in Korea: A Critical Evaluation of a Historical Theory |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23718816 |journal=Korean Studies |volume=5 |pages=109–128 |jstor=23718816 |issn=0145-840X}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last1=Barnes |first1=Gina |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.3998/mpub.18696 |title=Protohistoric Yamato |last2=Barnes |first2=Gina L. |date=1988 |publisher=U OF M CENTER FOR JAPANESE STUDIES |isbn=978-0-915703-11-1 |location=Ann Arbor, MI |pages=16–31|doi=10.3998/mpub.18696 }}</ref><ref name=":1" /> It suggests that northern Asian "horse-riders" influenced Japan in the [[4th century|4th]] and [[5th century|5th centuries]] CE. These horse-riders came from [[North Asia]] and the [[Korea|Korean peninsula]]. They conquered indigenous tribes in Japan. This led to the formation of the Yamato state. The theory is based on [[Horse tack|horse trappings]] found in [[Kofun|Japanese tombs]] from the [[Kofun period|Kofun Period]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" />

The Horse-Rider Theory was proposed by [[Egami Namio]] in 1948.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" />

== Overview ==
Fifth-century tombs from the Middle [[Kofun period]] (Kofun III) are large. They have many [[moat]]s and deposits of iron tools and weapons. Fewer [[bronze mirror]]s are found, and more tools appear. This shows a change in elite status symbols.<ref name=":0" />

The region saw changes in territory. Small political groups from the Early Kofun period joined under the Kawachi Court. This made the first regional political group called "[[Yamato Kingship|Yamato]]." Its base was in Kawachi. Many think Yamato started outside the [[Kinai|Kinai region]], likely from riders from Korea.<ref name=":0" />

There is evidence of [[Korean influence on Japanese culture]] during this period. Archaeology and genetics show this influence. The [[Imperial House of Japan|Japanese Imperial family]] mixed with Koreans. Japan had relations with the Korean state of [[Baekje]].<ref name=":1" /> Many historically known immigrants known as [[Toraijin]] arrived from Korea.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Rhee |first1=Song-nai |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctv20rsk33 |title=Archaeology and History of Toraijin: Human, Technological, and Cultural Flow from the Korean Peninsula to the Japanese Archipelago c. 800 BC–AD 600 |last2=Aikens |first2=C. Melvin |last3=Barnes |first3=Gina L. |date=2021 |publisher=Archaeopress|doi=10.2307/j.ctv20rsk33 |jstor=j.ctv20rsk33 }}</ref> Japan also traded with [[China]]. These interactions show cultural exchange in the region.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Cartwright |first=Mark |title=The Horse-rider Theory in Ancient Japan |url=https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1105/the-horse-rider-theory-in-ancient-japan/ |access-date=2023-11-10 |website=World History Encyclopedia |language=en}}</ref>

The idea of a Korean force conquering Japan is debated. The [[Nihon Shoki]], an 8th-century source, suggests a Japanese presence in Korea. This is now seen as unlikely. The influx of Korean goods and ideas into Japan did not result in a clear cultural change. This suggests a different form of [[Cultural diplomacy|cultural exchange]].<ref name=":1" />

== Criticism ==
Japanese historians challenge the Horse-Rider Theory. They point out issues with its timeline and evidence. They question the assumption that foreign goods mean military conquest. Korean historians argue for a cultural shift. They use changes in tombs and political structures as evidence. They also point to linguistic and mythological evidence.<ref name=":1" />

Many Japanese archaeologists challenge the theory. They say horse items appear too late to explain the early fifth-century tombs. Historians have other concerns. They question the focus on [[Central Asia]]n people and the interpretation of history.<ref name=":0" />

Others think the theory overemphasizes sudden change. They think slow cultural interactions make more sense. Some believe the state formed through cultural changes, not just one conquest event. Other ideas say the fifth-century changes came from conflicts with [[Kyushu]]. This led to new trade with Korea.<ref name=":0" />

Many historians propose interconnectedness between peoples across the Korean Straits without invasion or conquest. Migrations from Korea to Japan happened around 300 BCE. These migrations brought cultural and technological changes to Japan. This shows a cultural connection rather than separation between Korea and Japan.<ref name=":1" />
